heart: Check your blood pressure regularly — many people with hypertension feel fine until complications appear.
Aim for at least 150 minutes of moderate activity each week to support a healthier heart.
Cut back on salt. Excess sodium can raise blood pressure and strain your heart over time.
Include oily fish, nuts, and olive oil in your meals for heart-friendly fats.
If you smoke, quitting is one of the best things you can do for your cardiovascular health.
Manage stress with short daily breaks — chronic stress can affect blood pressure and heart rhythm.
Know your numbers: blood pressure, cholesterol, blood sugar, and BMI matter for heart risk.
Limit sugary drinks. High sugar intake is linked to weight gain and higher heart disease risk.
Get enough sleep. Poor sleep is associated with higher blood pressure and heart strain.
Walk after meals when you can — light movement helps blood sugar and circulation.
Eat more fibre from vegetables, beans, and whole grains to support cholesterol balance.
Take prescribed heart medications at the same time every day unless your doctor advises otherwise.
Watch for warning signs like chest pain, sudden shortness of breath, or unusual fatigue — seek care early.
Keep a healthy weight range that your clinician recommends for your body and conditions.
Schedule routine check-ups even when you feel well — prevention protects your heart.
child: Keep your child’s vaccination card up to date and bring it to every clinic visit.
Exclusive breastfeeding for the first 6 months supports immunity and healthy growth when possible.
Wash hands often — especially before meals and after using the toilet — to reduce infections.
Offer water instead of sugary drinks to protect teeth and lower obesity risk.
Create a consistent sleep routine; children need enough rest for growth and learning.
Supervise play near water, roads, and cooking areas to prevent common childhood injuries.
Introduce complementary foods gradually from 6 months while continuing breast milk or formula as advised.
Watch for dehydration signs during diarrhoea: dry mouth, fewer wet nappies, and unusual sleepiness.
Use insecticide-treated nets in malaria-endemic areas to protect infants and young children.
Limit screen time and encourage outdoor play for physical and social development.
Teach children to cover coughs and sneezes to reduce the spread of respiratory infections.
Store medicines and cleaning products out of children’s reach at all times.
Ensure your child gets vitamin A and deworming treatments according to local health guidelines.
Respond calmly to fever, but seek urgent care if a baby under 3 months has fever.
Celebrate small healthy habits — praise for handwashing and finishing meals builds lifelong routines.
pregnancy: Start prenatal visits early and keep every scheduled appointment for you and your baby.
Take folic acid as advised before and during early pregnancy to support neural tube development.
Stay hydrated and eat balanced meals with iron-rich foods to help prevent anaemia.
Avoid alcohol, smoking, and unprescribed drugs throughout pregnancy.
Rest when you can, and sleep on your side in later pregnancy if that is more comfortable.
Track baby movements daily in the third trimester and report reduced movement promptly.
Ask your clinician before taking any herbal remedies or over-the-counter medicines.
Wear comfortable shoes and elevate your feet if swelling becomes uncomfortable.
Practice gentle activity like walking unless your provider has advised otherwise.
Prepare a birth plan and know the nearest facility that can handle emergencies.
Watch for danger signs: severe headache, blurred vision, heavy bleeding, or severe abdominal pain.
Get screened for infections and conditions recommended in your antenatal package.
Eat small frequent meals if nausea is strong, and seek help if you cannot keep fluids down.
Discuss your mental health openly — anxiety and low mood in pregnancy deserve support.
After delivery, attend postnatal checks and continue iron and nutrition advice as recommended.
mental: Talk to someone you trust when stress feels heavy — connection is a form of care.
Take short breaks during the day; even five quiet minutes can reset your mind.
Limit late-night scrolling if it disrupts sleep — rest strongly affects mood.
Move your body regularly; walking can reduce tension and improve mental clarity.
Write down three things that went okay today to build a more balanced perspective.
Set boundaries with work and social media when you feel overwhelmed.
Seek professional help early if sadness, worry, or sleep problems last for weeks.
Avoid using alcohol to cope with stress — it often worsens anxiety and sleep.
Practice slow breathing: inhale for 4 counts, exhale for 6, repeat for a few minutes.
Keep a consistent wake and sleep time to support emotional stability.
Spend time outdoors when possible; natural light can lift energy and mood.
Celebrate small wins. Progress in mental health is often gradual, not sudden.
If thoughts of self-harm appear, contact emergency services or a crisis line immediately.
Reduce caffeine late in the day if it makes you restless or anxious.
Remember that asking for help is strength, not weakness.
medication: Take medicines exactly as prescribed — do not skip doses or double up without advice.
Use a pill organiser or phone reminder if you manage multiple medications.
Never share prescription drugs; what helps one person can harm another.
Tell your clinician about all medicines and supplements you take to avoid interactions.
Store medicines in a cool, dry place away from children and direct sunlight.
Check expiry dates before use and dispose of expired medicines safely.
Finish antibiotic courses as directed unless your clinician tells you to stop.
Ask your pharmacist how to take each medicine — with food, water, or at night.
Report unusual side effects early instead of silently stopping treatment.
Keep a written list of your medications for emergencies and clinic visits.
Do not crush or split tablets unless a pharmacist confirms it is safe.
Avoid buying medicines from unverified sources; counterfeit drugs are dangerous.
If you miss a dose, follow the label or ask a pharmacist — guessing can be risky.
Review long-term medications with your clinician at least once a year.
Bring empty packs or photos of your medicines to appointments for accurate reconciliation.
nutrition: Fill half your plate with vegetables and fruits for fibre, vitamins, and lasting energy.
Choose water as your main drink; sugary beverages add calories without much nutrition.
Include protein at meals — beans, eggs, fish, lean meat, or dairy support muscle and repair.
Cook with less oil and prefer boiling, steaming, or grilling when you can.
Read labels for salt and sugar content, especially in packaged snacks and sauces.
Eat slowly and stop when comfortably full to support digestion and portion control.
Add local leafy greens like ugu, spinach, or kale to stews and soups regularly.
Limit deep-fried street foods if you are watching cholesterol or weight.
Choose whole grains such as oats, brown rice, or whole-wheat bread more often.
Plan simple meals ahead to reduce reliance on ultra-processed convenience foods.
Include healthy snacks like fruit, yoghurt, or unsalted nuts between long gaps in meals.
Reduce salt gradually so your taste buds adjust without feeling deprived.
Stay consistent rather than perfect — small daily food choices compound over time.
If you have diabetes, pair carbohydrates with protein or fibre to steady blood sugar.
Ask a clinician before starting restrictive diets, especially if you are pregnant or unwell.
fitness: Start where you are: a 10-minute walk today is better than waiting for a perfect routine.
Warm up before intense activity and cool down afterward to reduce injury risk.
Mix cardio and strength training across the week for balanced fitness.
Use stairs when safe and practical — small movement adds up.
Stretch tight muscles gently after workouts, especially hips, calves, and shoulders.
Stay hydrated before, during, and after exercise, especially in hot weather.
Listen to pain signals; sharp pain is a reason to stop and reassess.
Set realistic weekly goals instead of extreme daily targets you cannot sustain.
Invite a friend to walk or exercise with you for accountability and enjoyment.
Include rest days so muscles can recover and performance can improve.
Strengthen your core with simple planks or bridges to support posture and balance.
Track progress by how you feel and what you can do, not only by weight.
Wear supportive shoes that fit well for walking or running.
If you have a chronic condition, ask your clinician which activities are safest.
Make movement social or musical — enjoyment is the best long-term motivator.
infectious: Wash hands with soap and water for at least 20 seconds before eating and after toilets.
Keep vaccinations current for yourself and your household according to local schedules.
Cover coughs and sneezes with a tissue or your elbow to limit droplet spread.
Drink clean, safe water and store it in covered containers.
Cook meat thoroughly and reheat leftovers until steaming hot.
Use insecticide-treated nets and clear standing water to reduce mosquito-borne disease risk.
Avoid self-medicating with antibiotics for viral illnesses like colds and flu.
Stay home when you have fever and contagious symptoms if you can, to protect others.
Clean and cover wounds promptly to prevent bacterial infection.
Practice safe sex and get tested when recommended to protect sexual health.
Dispose of waste properly and keep living spaces clean to reduce disease vectors.
Seek care early for persistent fever, severe diarrhoea, or difficulty breathing.
Follow isolation and treatment advice fully when diagnosed with an infectious disease.
Ensure food vendors handle food hygienically, or choose carefully prepared meals.
Teach children infection-prevention habits early — handwashing is a lifelong skill.
